content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an automatically learnt data augmentation module to perform mixing of images and corresponding labels. The paper shows improvements over existing mixing-based data augmentation methods and speedups to saliency-aware methods. TransformMix provides a good tradeoff - inference is as fast as "blind mixing" methods but saliency preservation of the augmented images is comparable to stronger data mixing augmentation baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The method performs faster than other saliency-based methods, which may be useful from a practical standpoint. 
2. Using a learnt transform over ad-hoc patch stitching can be useful for adapting to different datasets and preserve the natural smoothness of images.

Weaknesses:
1. The method is not very compellingly motivated, especially compared to the saliency-based methods. Transportation plans are similar to that in PuzzleMix, but the method uses an STN to combine images instead of blocking. The usage of teacher network is also explored in Supermix, and the novelty comes from the usage of STN for combining the data. 
2. The STN in the paper uses a rather limited capacity transformation which is an affine transform - most of the augmented images look like the saliency regions stacked next to each other. How does a crop+hstack/vstack augmentation work compared to TransformMix?
3. Experimental setup is not very satisfactory. Results in Table 2 are very similar to existing works. But, Tables 3 and 4 do not compare to Saliency/Super/Puzzle Mix baselines, which are saliency aware and should provide better insights to which transformations are more transferable, rather than comparing with Mixup and Cutmix which are "blind" baselines. Table 5 is hard to evaluate without any sort of error bars since the test-set accuracy are very close. How does the augmentation scale to bigger datasets, since these datasets would be big "stress test" for data augmentation methods?
4. Due to the experimental setup, it is not verified whether Saliency/Puzzle/Super Mix have good transfer capabilities, but Table1 mentions that they are not transferable. 
5. One of the things that is not very well explained is the fact that the algorithm is simultaneously trying to discover a mixing strategy for a particular dataset, but at the same time test its transferability on unseen images (which means the augmentation strategy doesn't exploit the particular structure of the source dataset). What kinds of tradeoffs can one see here? What are the implications on transferability of an augmentation strategy as the domain gap between the source and target datasets increase? 
6. One of the claims about extending the method for mixing more than two images can be applied to all the baselines mentioned in the paper. Therefore, the "Mix 3 or more images" row in Table 1 is not necessary since every method can be extended to K images.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback. We clarified our contributions and added more experiments. (1/2)
content.comment:
__1. The method is not very compellingly motivated.__
- Thanks for pointing this out. SuperMix uses a teacher network to optimize the mixing masks, while PuzzleMix optimizes the transport plans and mixing masks.  Compared to SuperMix, TransformMix learns to preserve the salient information by transforming the input images. Compared to PuzzleMix, TransformMix creates more visually compelling images that are more aligned with the natural image prior.
- In terms of novelty, the proposed two-phase training for sample-mixing, i.e. training a mixing module and then utilizing it to mix new unseen data, is first being proposed. Although TransformMix uses transformations and teacher networks, the framework trains a learnable mixing module instead of solving an optimization problem for each image pair, like SuperMix and PuzzleMix. Because of this careful design, TransfromMix can transfer the learning from a pre-training dataset and achieve approximately 4 times speed-up when mixing data.
- In addition to using STN to combine images instead of blocking, conventional STNs predict the transformation for a single image based on the raw image, while the STN in TransformMix predicts the transformations for multiple images at once based on their saliency maps, a sampled noise and mixing ratios. This is a new way of using STN.

__2. The STN in the paper uses a rather limited capacity transformation which is an affine transform – most of the augmented images look like the saliency regions stacked next to each other. How does a crop+hstack/vstack augmentation work compared to TransformMix?__

- Most images in CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 are aligned in the center so they can be separated by simple crop+hstack/vstack. However, such a simple augmentation may not work in TinyImageNet and ImageNet as the random cropping or stacking may occlude the salient regions of the image.  In Appendix G, we illustrate more visual examples of the predicted mixing masks and transformations. The visual examples demonstrate how the predicted masks adapt to the shapes and regions of the objects.
- We would also like to emphasize that TransformMix is an automated framework for learning the optimal transformation and mixing strategy. Although the simple manual crop+hstack/vstack may find to be effective on some datasets, it may not generalize well to other unseen datasets. On the contrary, TransformMix is saliency-aware and learns the optimal mixing strategy from the dataset automatically. In this perspective, TransformMix is more scalable and transferable to unseen data.

__3.1 The experimental setup is not very satisfactory. The results in Table 2 are very similar to existing works.__
Admittedly, the results in direct classification are comparable to existing works in terms of top-1 accuracy. However, TransformMix consistently provides non-trivial improvements in the top-5 accuracy on multiple datasets. Also, our method is approximately 4 times more efficient than the previous works as shown in Table 5 in section 4.5. Moreover, our proposed method outperforms other methods in the transfer fine-tuning experiments [see Table 3]. We believe that these are valid improvements over existing works.

__3.2 Table 5 is hard to evaluate without any sort of error bars since the test-set accuracy are very close.__

We added the error bars accordingly.

__3.3 How does the augmentation scale to bigger datasets?__

Due to limited computing power and time, the largest dataset we tested was ImageNet-1K. We believe other related works, e.g. PuzzleMix and SuperMix, were not evaluated on datasets bigger than ImageNet-1k.
We also observe that data augmentation tends to bring more benefits on smaller datasets where there is limited data. Instead of testing our method on bigger datasets, we conduct the fine-tuning experiments on four fine-grained classification datasets – Flower, Pet Car and Aircraft datasets. These datasets typically have a large number of classes but few samples per class. We believe that this setting is more challenging than CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet, which contains more samples per class. We hope this can demonstrate the effectiveness of TransformMix in more difficult tasks.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback. We clarified our contributions and added more experiments. (2/2)
content.comment:
__3.4 & 4. Tables 3 and 4 do not compare to Saliency/Super/Puzzle Mix baselines. It is not verified whether Saliency/Puzzle/Super Mix have good transfer capabilities, but Table1 mentions that they are not transferable.__

Thanks for pointing this out. We added stronger baselines to the transfer experiments and revised Table 1.

- The transfer task fine-tunes an ImageNet pre-trained model on four downstream tasks. SuperMix cannot be applied in this setting as it relies on the supervision signals of the teacher models trained on the actual downstream tasks to optimize the mixing masks. 

- In order to compare the transfer capabilities of different baselines, we added SaliencyMix and PuzzleMix to the transfer fine-tuning tasks. The updated Table 3 shows that TransformMix outperforms stronger PuzzleMix and SaliencyMix in the Pet, Car and Aircraft datasets and is comparable with PuzzleMix in the Flower dataset. We also revised Table 1 accordingly.

__Table 3__: Test-set Top-1 / Top-5 accuracy (%) for fine-tuning a pre-trained network to the Flower, Pet, Car and Aircraft datasets using the mixing module learned from CIFAR-100.

|              | Flower                | Pet                   | Car                   | Aircraft              |
|--------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| Simple       | 97.55 / __99.87__     | 92.88 / 99.48         | 79.43 / 95.52         | 68.79 / 92.34         |
| Mixup        | 97.92 / 99.75         | 93.04 / 99.31         | 80.84 / 95.77         | 70.83 / 93.00         |
| CutMix       | 97.67 / 99.63         | 92.09 / 99.20         | 80.91 / 95.94         | 69.63 / 93.06         |
| SaliencyMix  | 98.16 / 99.75         | 92.83 / 99.34         | 78.90 / 95.32         | 69.42 / 92.25         |
| PuzzleMix    | __98.28__ / 99.75     | 92.66 / __99.50__     | 80.62 / 95.87         | 70.89 / 92.97         |
| TransformMix | 98.16 / __99.87__     | __93.34__ / __99.50__ | __82.11__ / __96.48__ | __72.36__ / __93.12__ |
|              | $\pm$0.06 / $\pm$0.06 | $\pm$0.13 / $\pm$0.04 | $\pm$0.47 / $\pm$0.18 | $\pm$0.35 / $\pm$0.16 |
 
__5. What kinds of tradeoffs can one see in the transfer setting? What are the implications on the transferability of an augmentation strategy as the domain gap between the source and target datasets increases?__

- In our experiments, we found that the direct case (i.e. training the mixing module on a dataset and applying the discovered mixing strategy on the same dataset) performs the best. In the transfer setting, e.g. CIFAR-10 -> ImageNet, there is a slight drop in the accuracy [see Table 8 in Appendix C]. However, as a trade-off of the accuracy, TransformMix can transfer the mixing strategy from a pre-trained dataset to predict the mixing mask and transformation in one forward pass, which makes it more efficient than other saliency-aware methods, like SuperMix and PuzzleMix. 

- To enhance the transferability, the mixing module of TransformMix is conditioned on saliency maps instead of image features. We believe that the saliency maps of the images from different datasets share similar structures. Therefore, the learned mixing strategy from a source dataset can be transferred to other target datasets. However, we agree that if the saliency maps of the target datasets happen to be very different from the source dataset, e.g., the images of the source dataset contain single objects but the images of the target dataset contain multiple objects, the drop in end accuracy may be more significant. 

__6. The "Mix 3 or more images" row in Table 1 is not necessary since every method can be extended to K images.__

Thanks for pointing this out. We removed the "Mix 3 or more images" row in Table 1.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an automated approach, TransformMix, to learn appropriate data augmentation for the target tasks. With the proposed mixing module ad mixing masks, TransformMix demonstrates state-of-the-art results and good performance in transfer learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
* This paper provides diagrams, highlighting the differences between the proposed TransformMix and the existing sample-mixing data augmentation methods.
* This paper obtains the state-of-the-art on several benchmarks and demonstrates good transferring performance on downstream tasks.
* TransformMix is faster than previous sample-mixing data augmentation methods.

**Weaknesses**
* This paper only generalizes the proposed method on classification benchmarks. The generalization ability on other downstream tasks, such as object detection on coco, is unknown.
* Insufficient citations and discussions about current sample-mixing methods, including but not limited to [1], [2], [3], etc.
* Minor: It is suggested to move the training cost/speedup comparisons into the main text and supplement missing related works, e.g. the aforementioned ones.

[1] Venkataramanan, Shashanka et al. “AlignMixup: Improving Representations By Interpolating Aligned Features.” 2022 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) (2022): 19152-19161.    
[2] Qin, Jie et al. “ResizeMix: Mixing Data with Preserved Object Information and True Labels.” ArXiv abs/2012.11101 (2020): n. pag.     
[3] Hong, Minui et al. “StyleMix: Separating Content and Style for Enhanced Data Augmentation.” 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) (2021): 14857-14865.

content.title: Thank your for your suggestions. We added the knowledge distillation experiment and supplemented the mentioned related works.
content.comment:
__This paper only generalizes the proposed method on classification benchmarks.__

Thanks for your suggestion. The related works, like SuperMix and PuzzleMix, mainly compare the results in classification tasks but not object detection tasks. As suggested by reviewer a18R, we compare TransformMix with SuperMix on the knowledge distillation task in Table 10. We follow the SuperMix experiment, which uses a WRN-40-2 teacher model to provide the supervision signals for training a ShuffleNetV1 student model on the CIFAR-100 dataset with TransformMix augmentation. Despite the efforts to reproduce the results, we could not fully replicate the baseline performance. In our experiments, TransformMix improves the accuracy by 7.52% and 0.63% over the student model trained with no sample-mixing and MixUp, respectively. The gains are comparable to the reported results in SuperMix. We hope this can demonstrate the effectiveness of TransformMix beyond classification tasks.

__Table 10__: Top-1 test accuracy of the student model trained using knowledge distillation method on CIFAR-100.
|              | Teacher Acc. | Student Acc. | w/ MixUp | w/ Method | Gain over Student Acc. / MixUp |
|--------------|--------------|--------------|----------|-----------|--------------------------------|
| SuperMix     | 75.61        | 70.50        | 77.44    | 78.07     | 7.57 / 0.63                    |
| TransfromMix | 75.59        | 69.24        | 76.24    | 76.76     | 7.52 / 0.52                    |

__Insufficient citations and discussions about current sample-mixing methods.__
Thanks for pointing this out. Initially, we considered PuzzleMix and SuperMix as the most closely related works as PuzzleMix separates the saliency region and SuperMix uses a teacher model. However, for the completeness of the study, we added the suggested sample-mixing works in the related work section.

__Minor: It is suggested to move the training cost/speedup comparisons into the main text.__
Thanks for your suggestion. We moved the training cost comparisons into the main text.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new method for mixing up images, such that the mixed images form a more effective training dataset. Mixing training points during training has been shown to be quite effective in previous papers, starting with the mixup paper. TransformMix is a more advanced and complicated way of mixing images, where the saliency maps are used to construct visually more meaningful samples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- TransformMix seems to lead to more natural looking mixed images.
- The use of saliency for augmentations make sense. 
- Augmentation transfer results look impressive. 

Weaknesses:

- The reported performance of the selected baselines seems low. This method is an incremental improvement over the many previous methods building on mixup. It is possible for a paper to be of interest to ICLR audience with an incremental technical improvement, but then the empirical evaluation becomes all the more important. Does the row labelled "Simple" on Table 2 refer to training with just flips and crops? If so, 76.1% is a standard number ResNet-50 can reach in 90 epochs, but the authors report 75.69%.  
- For example, the authors report 77.01% for ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet with mixup. However, the original Mixup paper reports 77.9% accuracy for 200 epoch training and 76.7% accuracy for 90 epoch training. If I understood correctly, authors have trained their mixing module on Imagenet for 100 epochs, and then trained the classifier on ImageNet for another 100 epochs. Which should be the correct baseline for Mixup, 77.9 or 76.7?  A related question is, does TransformMix perform as well as regular Mixup when trained for 200 epochs? 
- The authors seem to have skipped comparison to strong baselines. For example, AutoMix is cited in the submission, but I did not see any comparison to the AutoMix numbers. AutoMix is similarly a complicated improvement over Mixup, and comparing to its results directly would be expected.

content.comment:
__The reported performance of the selected baselines seems low.__

Thanks for pointing this out. Admittedly, the results in direct classification are comparable to existing works in terms of top-1 accuracy. However, TransformMix consistently provides non-trivial improvements in the top-5 accuracy on multiple datasets. Also, our method is approximately 4 times more efficient than the previous works as shown in Table 5 in section 4.5. Moreover, our proposed method outperforms other methods in the transfer fine-tuning experiments [see Table 3]. We believe that these are valid improvements over existing works.

__Difference in reported ImageNet baselines.__

The “Simple” baseline uses just flips and crops. We follow the training protocol proposed by PuzzleMix for more efficient ImageNet training. Specifically, the training resizes ImageNet images to smaller resolutions during different phases of training. This may cause a slight drop in the end classification accuracy. We would like to clarify that all the baselines are trained using the prescribed efficient training protocol, and our experimental results match the results reported by PuzzleMix.

__Farier baseline for MixUp.__

Thanks for pointing this out. We agree that our proposed TransformMix demands more training efforts in the direct classification setting (i.e. 100 epochs training the mixing module + 100 epochs training the classifier.) To mitigate this concern, we reduced the pre-training epochs to 5 epochs instead of 100 epochs. We find that the mixing module can learn an effective mixing strategy despite the reduced pre-training epochs. Specifically, the accuracy of TransformMix with reduced pre-training epochs on ImageNet is 77.58, and the MixUp baseline is 77.01. We hope this makes a fairer comparison between TransformMix and Mixup trained for 100 epochs. 

__The authors seem to have skipped the comparison to strong baselines.__

Thank you for your suggestion. We added stronger baselines to show the effectiveness of TransformMix:
- Initially, we did not consider AutoMix because it uses a different training setting from other baselines, and there is no code available. replying_to: Replying to Thank you for your constructive feedback. We clarified the experimental results and added stronger baselines.
display_title: thanks for the clarifications and additional results

content.title: thanks for the clarifications and additional results
content.comment:
Re: the training setting of PuzzleMix

Thanks for the clarification, I acknowledge that baselines are lower than standard training setting because all baselines as well as all TransformMix runs have been conducted with a cheaper but less accurate training protocol. Could the authors clarify if this is because TransformMix mainly works well with this cheaper protocol? Or is it because authors only had the resources to run all the experiments under this cheap setting? Either option could be fine, but I would be curious about a clarification on this point. If it is the latter, could the authors do a few of the experiments with more standard settings to show that their improvements hold under this setting as well? For example, a ResNet-50 trained on Imagenet (with just flips and crops) can achieve 76.1% or more easily. 

I think this distinction is important, and some regularization methods can have more outsized impact on substandard baselines compared to standard baselines. 

Re: Mixup baselines

I have a similar question about the Mixup baseline. Authors only compare to the 100-epoch baseline. Is this because TransformMix helps 90 epoch training more than Mixup but not the 180 or more epoch training? If this is the case, TransformMix could still be useful, but it'd be good to have this information in the paper. If TransformMix can actually outperform Mixup just as much or more in 180 epochs, I think this would also be good to include in the paper. Stronger data augmentation methods such as Mixup are often used with longer training, and it would be important to show the performance of TransformMix under this setting at least for this Imagenet Mixup baseline.

To summarize, I appreciate the authors' perspective that they followed PuzzleMix protocol for all evaluations which makes the evaluations fair. But it is also important for evaluations to be relevant, and I believe including the standard Resnet-50 baseline of 76.1% with flip crops and Mixup training of 180+ epochs would improve the relevance of the evaluations in this paper. 

I also wanted to acknowledge that the authors found they were getting about as good results with 5 epochs of augmentation pretraining as they do with 100 epochs. This seems like a major improvement, perhaps a bit surprising, and I do wonder if it implies something important about the TransformMix approach. Maybe this particular observation can be studied by the authors or other researchers in a followup paper.

| Mixup        | 97.92 / 99.75         | 93.04 / 99.31         | 80.84 / 95.77         | 70.83 / 93.00         |

__2-- Could the authors provide results on tasks such as knowledge distillation and object detection?__

Thanks for your suggestion. The related works, like SuperMix and PuzzleMix, mainly compare the results in classification tasks but not object detection tasks. As suggested by the reviewer, we compare TransformMix with SuperMix on the knowledge distillation task in Table 10. We follow the SuperMix experiment, which uses a WRN-40-2 teacher model to provide the supervision signals for training a ShuffleNetV1 student model on the CIFAR-100 dataset with TransformMix augmentation. Despite the efforts to reproduce the results, we could not fully replicate the baseline performance. In our experiments, TransformMix improves the accuracy by 7.52% and 0.63% over the student model trained with no sample-mixing and MixUp, respectively. The gains are comparable to the reported results in SuperMix. We hope this can demonstrate the effectiveness of TransformMix beyond classification tasks.

| SuperMix     | 75.61        | 70.50        | 77.44    | 78.07     | 7.57 / 0.63                    |
| TransfromMix | 75.59        | 69.24        | 76.24    | 76.76     | 7.52 / 0.52                    |
